label: paragraph_title
text: END OF BOYCOTT.

label: text
text: CANTON'S LATEST DIFFICULTIES.

label: text
text: Taxes to Go to Strikers?

label: text
text: REPORTED THREAT OF USING. FORCE IF NECESSARY.

label: text
text: Optimism has not increased with regard to the proposed settlement of the Canton boycott and latest developments point to more difficulties for the Nationalist Government in their attempt to arrive at a solution.

label: text
text: Conditions at Lowu railway station, on the New Territory border are now the same as before, practically the full complement of strike pickets being on duty on the frontier.

label: text
text: Fresh difficulties—in addition to opposition by a minority of politicians—are confronting the Canton Government.

label: text
text: Passengers on the Kowloon-Canton Railway are now subjected to the same interference as in previous months.

label: text
text: One point that may further complicate the issue is the reported demand of the strikers for their share of the projected new taxes.

label: text
text:
Canton, Oct. 4.
Mr. Eugene Chen has informed the strikers that recommendation will be made to the Government to use force against opposition.

label: paragraph_title
text: Eugene Chen's Threat.

label: text
text: Li Cheung-tat, Police "Commissioner, has sent out additional armed patrols to prevent unlawful acts by labourers.

label: text
text:
The Seamen's Union has asked that to settle the boycott all men previously employed on ships between Hong Kong and Canton to be reinstated.—Wah Tsz Yat Po.
To Last 8 Months.

label: text
text: Besides their claim to an interest in the import, luxury and export levies, the strikers are asking for a Government allocation of $10,000 a month as assistance.

label: text
text: Another request is that the Government, the Strike Executive "and all classes" co-operate to form

label: text
text: employment agencies to facilitate the return to work of strikers, the quota to be 3,000 per month, each man on returning to work to be presented with a $100 bonus by the Government as recognition for the "share in the victory."

label: text
text: This scheme is to last for eight months, it is stated, when the movement will be entirely ended. "Meanwhile, the strikers ask that dormitories and free meals continue as hitherto "until a big scheme can be devised to effect a settlement."

label: text
text: Strikers' Attitude.

label: text
text:
Another query that is given by rumour is that strikers are now asking? what about the several millions of dollars allocated by the Government to pay us off?
So Shiu-ching, chairman of the Strike Executive, is reported to have expressed their attitude as fully supporting the Government in terminating the strike, present strike institutions will be continued and an interest in the new taxes.

label: text
text: "On the face of things, little has developed" to show which way the wind is blowing.

label: text
text: Each day brings added strength to the opinion that the Canton Government will call off armed pickets to restore communications, but that the real boycott will continue and that the pickets will function under some other name as plain-clothes men.

label: text
text:
Shanghai Comment
Commenting in an editorial on October 1 (when it was assumed in Shanghai that the Canton boy-cott had terminated), the "N.-C. Daily News" observes:—

label: text
text: “The point to emphasise is that the Canton Government, by calling off the boycott when it suited their purpose to do so, have openly confessed that the boycott was always theirs to maintain or terminate as they pleased. Mr. Eugene Chen's phrase about ‘arrangements with the Strike Committee’ (if possible to-day, why not months ago?) is mere camouflage.

label: text
text: “This is one of the most unblushing admissions of past duplicity that could be found.”

label: text
text: "Hitherto the Canton Government have always pretended that the boycott was the spontaneous expression of a virtuously enraged people, which they were powerless to prevent."

label: text
text: "And more than once negotiators from Hong Kong have been referred to the Strike Committee on the excuse that the affair was none of the Canton Government's."

label: text
text: "All this is now conveniently forgotten on the Cantoness side Not so, however, on the foreign especially in view of the hard!"

label: text
text: vailed threat in Mr. Eugene Chen's last sentence.

label: text
text: "If there is any revival of the boycott, Hong Kong will know exactly why.....there could be no longer any pretence of shifting the responsibility. And what it has suited the Canton Government to take off, they must not be allowed to reimpose."

label: text
text:
Goodwill & the Future.
On Canton—foreign relations the
"N. C. Daily News" says:—

label: text
text: "Quite apart from the threat involved, there is a touch of seriousness, even of pathos, in Mr. Eugene Chen's allusion to 'British comprehension of Chinese nationalism, Its ideas and force as a principle of energy in the work of unifying and modernising China,' which will appeal to all who strive to read the signs of the times."

label: text
text: "Britons have no cause just now to love the Canton Government, whose duplicity, and deceitfulness have done more harm than Chinese are aware of in embittering old kindly feelings and imparting a hardness to foreign thoughts of this country where once there was only goodwill."

label: text
text: "But while we turn in disgust from so much that Canton" has done, it would be unwise and unjust to depreciate the force and potential value of the nationalist movement.

label: paragraph_title
text: Break From the Past.

label: text
text: "In Canton are numbers of earnest men and women, whose ambitions for their country are worthy of respect, even though their efforts are liable at the outset to go astray and to give an impression of themselves as displeasing as it is really inaccurate."

label: text
text: "And this same nationalist spirit is at work in varying degrees in all parts of China. It is the one source of energy and life to which she can look for the future and foreigners must learn to look to it also....".

label: text
text: "There is something monstrous in the perversity of it all from which one would pain break away to make a new start, forgetting the past and determined only to do the best for the future. It will not be Great Britain's fault if the lifting of the boycott in Canton does not prove the'starting point of a new era.'"

label: text
text: As the “China Mail” explained at the time, there can be no two views on Canton's proposed new taxes, says the “N. C. Daily News”:—

label: text
text: “Acceptance or rejection of this proposal does not depend on Great Britain alone, but is a question for all the Powers. This should clearly be understood.

label: text
text: "No Power could act alone in such a change, without detriment to her nationals; and the full scheme to include abolition of likin necessarily requires the acquiescence of all Powers."

label: text
text: "Speaking generally, we see no reason why they should not agree. The extra taxation is not heavy; not the merchant, but the consumer would pay; and he should not feel it greatly."

label: text
text: Canton's Expensive Failure.

label: text
text: "The question is whether the Powers would be willing to do in one district what they are not yet doing, though they are quite ready to do it, in all China....."

label: text
text: "In all probability the Canton Government realised that, whatever harm it (the boycott) might be doing to Hong Kong, it was a highly expensive failure from Canton's point of view and contributed to a state of lawlessness most undesirable while General Chang Kaf-shek was conducting a life-and-death campaign in the north."

label: paragraph_title
text: LATEST PIRACY.

label: paragraph_title
text: H. K. SEAPLANE IN PURSUIT.

label: paragraph_title
text: Shanghai Steamer on the Way

label: text
text: The China Merchants S. N. Co.'s s.s. "Hsinfung" has been pirated at Bias Bay.

label: text
text: Only mengre details are to hand at the moment but there seems no room for doubt.

label: text
text: As in the case of the "Kwang Lee" (of the same company), the steamer was on the Shanghai-Canton direct run.

label: text
text: In pre-strike times these boats called at Hong Kong en route, but this port is now omitted.

label: text
text: This morning, the China Navigation Co.'s s.s. "Szechuan" left Hong Kong for Amoy and Shanghai.

label: text
text: She wirelessed back a report that the "Hsinfung" had been seen to be pirated in Bias Bay, that hotbed of pirates in the province of Kwangtung.

label: text
text: On receipt of the message, the local Naval authorities despatched a seaplane to scout over the vicinity and report.

label: text
text: The “Szechuan” also indicated that the pirated steamer was on her way to Hong Kong but the local office of the China Merchants. Co. state that she may go round Hong Kong, direct to Canton, unless there are casualties on board which may need urgent medical attention.

label: paragraph_title
text: A. Surmise.

label: text
text:
The "Hstinfung," of course, is of the usual type of China. Merchants steamer. Before the strike, she occasionally called here, but was mostly on the northern runs.
Usually she carries six European officers, who are most likely to be British, but there are quite a number of Scandinavians in the company's employ.

label: text
text: The only opinion expressed so far is that the pirates shipped as passengers and followed the old-time modus operandi, subsequently bringing the vessel to Bias Bay to be looted.

label: text
text: Few European passengers travel by this route to Canton.

label: text
text: TO BE ADMIRAL

label: text
text: Vice-Admiral Sir Edwyn Sinclair Alexander-Sinclair, K.C.B., M.V.O., Commander-in-Chief, China Station, has been promoted to Admiral to date October 4, 1926.

label: text
text: Vice-Admiral Sir Alexander Sinclair has only been Commander-in-Chief of the China Station for little over a year. It will be remembered that he succeeded Vice Admiral Sir Allan Everett, who, only after a few months on the station, had to leave on account of ill-health and who has since gone on the retired list. Sir Alexander Sinclair who is the senior Vice-Admiral, is going to the Nore, in succession to Admiral Sir William Goodenough, and will be succeeded here by Vice-Admiral Sir Reginald Tyrwhitt.

label: paragraph_title
text: DESPERATE FIGHT.

label: paragraph_title
text: CANTONESE STAND THEIR GROUND.

label: paragraph_title
text: Deciding Battle at Moment.

label: paragraph_title
text: WAR CONTINUES BUT ARMISTICE QUITE POSSIBLE.

label: text
text: Latest despatches from the Kiangsi-Hupch war zone indicate that the southerners are now standing their ground and fighting desperately against Sun Chuan-fang, whose advance appears to have been stemmed.

label: text
text: The possibility of an armistice has become less remote: While at one place the rival armies are struggling zealously, other detachments on the same front are marking time.

label: text
text: [From Our Special Correspondent.]

label: text
text: The second battle of Kao. An is likely to prove the deciding engagement of the war.

label: text
text: At a vulnerable point in his line on the Kiangsi-Hunan front, General Chang Kai-shek has rushed up his best divisions and is now holding his ground.

label: text
text: The “5 province allies” under Marshal Sun Chuan-fang are still attacking and the fighting is very severe.

label: text
text: A little further north, that is in the Yangtse-Lake Tayeh sector, the southerners are under General Tang Sang-chee (8th army) and General Li Chungjen (7th army).

label: text
text: Bombardment Continues.

label: text
text: About 30,000 troops withdrawn from the pursuit against Wy Peifu, from Hankow and vicinity, and other places, have been moved eastwards to prevent Sun Chuanfang getting any nearer Wu-chang.

label: text
text: The bombardment, by the northern allies, continues at Hwang-chow, which is considered the key to Wuchang-hsien, the capital of Hupeh province which the Nationalists took from Wu Pei-fu.

label: text
text: In the south of Kiangsi, neither side is doing much and the allied commanders there still favour peace as the southerners have not vacated this part of their territory and they prefer to get it back without fighting.

label: text
text: Position Summed Up.

label: text
text: Summed up, the situation is: near Yangtse, the allies are still trying to push on to Wuchang and the 7th Canton army had difficulty in retiring from an advanced position. In the centre Chang Kai-shek has now given up, rearguard actions but is throwing his main strength in to divert attention from Wuchang. In the south, a comparative state of it is felt that the possibility of statemate prevails:

label: text
text: an armistice at this stage is less remote but the deciding battle may be over by this week.

label: text
text: Yesterday's report which gave the number of Canton prisoners taken by the allies as 5,000 is described as exaggerated. The total captures by Sun Chuan-fang are unlikely to exceed 3,000.

label: paragraph_title
text: OFFICIAL DESPATCH.

label: text
text: The following is published by courtesy of the Hong Kong Naval authorities:—

label: text
text:
Hankow, Oct. 4.
still holding out

label: text
text: An anti-British demonstration has been planned for tomorrow, Tuesday, but will probably not amount to much.

label: text
text: Southern flags are disappearing in the Chinese city and in the ex-Russian Concession and there is a general feeling that the northerners will be back here shortly.

label: text
text: Heavy fighting is reported between Wang Shih-ko and Hwang-chow; the former is held by the northerners and the latter by the southerners.

label: text
text: It is reported that a big drive towards Nanchang will be made by the southerners to relieve the pressure on Hankow.

label: text
text: General Yang Sen is sending large forces to Ichang and Shash against the southerners.

label: text
text: There has been indiscriminate firing on ships in the neighbourhood of Hwang-chow.

label: text
text: A British gunboat with the Ice-Consul on board is proceeding there to-morrow, Tuesday, and will convoy ships.

label: text
text: The negotiations following the Wanhlen affair are proceeding smoothly. The British Consul and gunboats have exchanged

label: text
text: calls with General Yang Sen and are expected to leave for Chungking to-morrow, Tuesday.

label: paragraph_title
text: DESERVED CONFIDENCE.

label: text
text: "When you next write to Shanghai about this situation," said one of Marshal Sun Chuangfang's staff officers in parting yesterday, "please be cheerful about it. Tell the people that we cannot possibly lose that with Chang Kai-shek being pushed back into Honan we have broken the Red advance, and that the conclusion of this campaign is coming quickly and surely. It would surprise none of us if the Cantonese were in full retreat before a letter could reach Shanghai."

label: text
text: This sanguine statement was the conclusion of an attempted interview with Marshal Sun Chuang-fang on the China Merchants' str. "Kingfishin" at Ki-kiang.

label: text
text: It may sound over-confident, but it does no more than confirm the general impression that one gets coming down the river; after getting well away from pessimistic and poorly informed Hankow.

label: paragraph_title
text: In Steel Helmets.

label: text
text: The first surprise that one gets is the spectacle of the striped flag flying over Huangshihkang, the port for Tayen, and of great numbers of steel helmetted northern soldiers on the foreshore.

label: text
text: From this point down to Wusueh one sees tented encampments of the northerners at every little settlement and then at Wusueh there is General Chen Tiao-yuan's big concentration.

label: text
text: In Kuukiang one finds the community in the grasp of a very well equipped and seemingly serious and business-like soldier who inspire confidence at a glance.

label: text
text: The general plan of campaign is to drive westward from various points in Kiangsi, in several columns, towards the Hukuang railway, and the Siang river and thereby endanger the Red line of communications and force their withdrawal from Hupeh and northern Hunan.

label: text
text: If carried out swiftly enough this withdrawal will of necessity be a rout, since the Cantonese and Humaneese Reds have gone so far afield over routes in which communications are bad. If they have to run to get back before being cut off, it is assumed that there will be no great difficulty about keeping them running well into southern Hunan and over the Kwangtung border.

label: text
text: Apart from the Shantung Brigade at Huangshihkang and the outposts along the river, there is no force above Wusueh and there is, as yet, no thought of a direct advance upon the Wu-Han cities by the river route.

label: text
text: The big fight, however, in the sight of both parties, is that being waged between Nanchang and Pinghsiang, with Chang Kai-shek and his two best Cantonese divisions, including the Whampoa Cadets, on the one hand, and Governor Lu Hsiang-ting, with five brigades of Chekiang troops and several brigades of Kiangsi troops on the other.

label: text
text: If Chang is badly defeated in this quarter, his whole expedition is a wreck and the Hunanese and Cantonese north of Changzh will be helpless refugees in an alien land.
